title: The Spirit prays (Romans 8:26–27)
hook: we don't know how to pray, and the Spirit asks for us with groanings

segments.voice: Yesterday, the good I would, and the evil I would not. Your line was who shall deliver me. Did you name the gap honestly? Day five hundred sixty-five.

A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. Someone you love is in surgery, and you want to pray, and you have no idea what to say. Heal them? Give me strength? Let it be quick? The words won't come. All you have is a long breath out, and maybe tears. If you've been there, Paul has something to tell you. You weren't failing to pray. Someone was praying with you.
screen: `A WAITING ROOM, 3 A.M.` → `NO WORDS COME.` → `ONLY A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: Romans 8 is often called the high point of the whole letter. After chapter seven's cry, who shall deliver me, chapter eight opens with no condemnation, and then it is full of the Spirit. Paul has just said that all creation groans, like a woman in labor, waiting. We groan too, he says, waiting. Then this: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." That's the King James. Notice three things. First, Paul includes himself: we know not what to pray for. The apostle whose name is on so many New Testament letters admits he doesn't always know how to pray. Second, the Spirit helps our infirmities, our weakness. The Greek verb pictures someone taking hold of the other end of a heavy load. You're not carrying it alone. Third, groanings which cannot be uttered. Too deep for words. The Spirit's own prayer sounds less like a speech and more like a sigh. And the next verse adds that God, who searches hearts, knows what the Spirit means, because the Spirit asks according to God's will. So the wordless sigh in the waiting room is not a failed prayer. In Paul's picture it may be the most honest prayer there is, carried by God within you to God. The Catechism quotes this passage when it calls the Holy Spirit the interior master of Christian prayer.
screen: `CREATION GROANS, AND SO DO WE.` · `WE KNOW NOT WHAT TO PRAY FOR.` · `THE SPIRIT TAKES THE OTHER END.` · `GROANINGS WHICH CANNOT BE UTTERED.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT PRAYS FOR US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sigh as a prayer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind whatever is heaviest right now, something you don't know how to pray about. Don't look for words. Breathe in slowly, and then let out a long sigh, out loud if you can. Let that sigh carry the whole thing. Do it again. If you pray, you can trust that the Spirit is praying in that breath, asking what you can't. If you don't, just notice how much a sigh can hold. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
The Spirit prays. When we don't know how to pray, the Spirit takes the other end of the load and prays in us with sighs too deep for words. Today's word.
Your line: the spirit prays for us. Today, when words run out, let one long sigh be your prayer. Day five hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics often begin prayer by asking the Holy Spirit's help, and the Church teaches that the Spirit is the interior teacher of prayer; many pray in silence, without words, before the Blessed Sacrament.

fork.setup: you're in a waiting room in the middle of the night. you want to pray and no words come. what do you do?
options: give up; it doesn't count without words.
let a sigh be the prayer.
look up the right prayer first.
fork.reveal: not graded. but Paul says the Spirit prays in us with groanings which cannot be uttered, and God knows what the Spirit means.

original.note: Greek: with groanings that cannot be spoken, sighs too deep for words.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is finding the right words.
what it means: when we don't know what to pray, the Spirit prays in us with sighs deeper than words, and God understands.
what a scholar hears: synantilambanetai, helpeth, pictures taking hold together on the other end of a load. the groaning echoes the groaning of creation and of believers just before.

notes: 13 of the 21 New Testament letters bear Paul's name; the script says 'so many'.
Synantilambanomai 'take hold together': standard lexicon sense; confirm.
CCC 2672 calls the Holy Spirit 'the interior Master of Christian prayer'; CCC 741 and 2630 cite Romans 8:26. Confirm.
